_why: Milestone 0.4. rule-diff.sh reports every per-rule count change between the
last release and this build. Reporting is not accountability: a drop and a
correct narrowing look identical in that output, and the only thing telling
them apart was whoever happened to read the job summary.
This file is the other half. Every rule whose count DROPS must have an entry
here saying why. An unexplained drop fails the job; so does an entry that no
longer describes a real drop, because a ledger nothing validates rots into
The baseline is the last released nox, so entries accumulate between releases
and are cleared when one is cut. `nox_release` records which release they are
written against: if it does not match the tag rule-diff resolved, the ledger
is stale as a whole and says so rather than silently passing.

classifications.duplicate-retired: a second rule reported the same condition; one ID was retired into the other, which carries the alias
classifications.applicability-narrowed: the rule does not apply to this subject or resource kind, and now says so
classifications.sanitizer-recognized: the value reaching the sink is neutralized for this vulnerability class
classifications.refined-away: a cheaper semantic fact refutes the candidate the pattern generated
classifications.rule-removed: the rule was deleted outright; no survivor reports the condition
classifications.context-narrowed: the rule's context requirement is now measured in characters as well as lines, so a keyword far away on the same physical line no longer qualifies as context
classifications.keyword-tokenized: the rule's vendor keyword must now be a token; it used to match as a bare substring, so it could be supplied by an accident inside opaque data or by an ordinary English word
classifications.format-bound: the rule now requires the vendor's real credential format; the value it matched is issued by that vendor but is not a credential
classifications.binding-required: the vendor name must now BIND the value through an assignment; sitting adjacent to a generic token is not evidence that the token is that vendor's credential

entries.reason: The bodies and response side of a recorded HTTP exchange are traffic, not a credential the repository holds — and nobody can rotate them. Measured by this harness against v1.39.2: 373 -> 0 on crewai-cassettes, and NO CHANGE across the other 24 repositories, which is the evidence the gate is scoped to recordings rather than over-reaching. The earlier figure of 522 -> 0 was against v1.35.0 and is not this change's marginal value: v1.38.2's 2048-character bound on entropy candidates and its word-boundary context hints had already removed 149 of them. Of the 540 SEC-161/SEC-162 findings read individually on crewAI, not one was a credential: 234 Cloudflare __cf_bm/_cfuvid cookies, 148 continuation lines of base64 response bodies, 58 response ids, 44 embedding vectors, 32 Gemini thought signatures, and 8 occurrences of PostHog's phc_ project key — which the vendor publishes and SEC-661 deliberately excludes, reported anyway by the generic entropy rule out of a recorded response body. The gate covers SEC-161 and SEC-162, the two rules whose whole claim is that some bytes are random; SEC-162 has no entry because it drops nothing on this corpus. Any rule encoding a vendor's credential format still fires anywhere in a recording, including a request body, which is where an OAuth client_secret sits. The request headers and URI are untouched, and SEC-082 was fixed in the same change so that an unredacted authorization header in a cassette is reported at all — it was not, because Go's \s crosses a newline but not a YAML sequence dash. See docs/design/recorded-http-exchanges.md.

A reference to where a secret is stored is not the secret, and SEC-080's own remediation tells you to write one. Measured against main on the 25-entry corpus: 12 -> 0, every drop read individually and every one a reference — 4 CloudFormation dynamic references ('{{resolve:secretsmanager:...}}'), 3 GitHub Actions secret references ("${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}"), 3 Ansible/Jinja variables ("{{ upassword }}"), and 2 shell variables ("$hashed_password") in .sh files. No other rule moved in any repository. Only a value that is ENTIRELY a reference qualifies: a quote inside the braces ({{ 'hunter2' }}, default('hunter2')) is a template evaluating to a hardcoded literal; a literal prefix or suffix could be the credential; an interpolation with a non-empty fallback (${PW:-hunter2}) is what runs when the variable is unset; and a bare $name is a reference only in a shell file, because YAML, JSON and Python do not expand it. Each of those is asserted still reportable, and the quote exclusion was falsified by removing it. placeholderCandidate's comment had claimed to handle "${SECRET}" since it was written; its regex, <[^>]*>, never matched one.

A file under __testfixtures__ is jscodeshift's input/output pair: the codemod's test reads it with readFileSync and runs a transform over the string, so its imports are the transform's subject matter, not a dependency, and nothing resolves or installs them. 109 -> 0 on vercel-ai-codemod, the same 109 on v1.39.2 (built from its tag) and on main; A/B against main, NO rule moves in the other 24 repositories. The dropped names are deliberately fictional — other-pkg, other-package, not-ai, some-other-package, other-module — written to prove the codemod leaves foreign imports alone, alongside real packages (@ai-sdk/openai, zod) that appear as fixture text. On a full vercel/ai checkout SLOP-001 goes 36 -> 3, the three being ordinary test scripts outside any fixture directory, still reported. Only a directory segment named exactly __testfixtures__ qualifies (a substring match was falsified by test), and each exempted import is recorded as a refutation.
